title: JSONB, upserts and MERGE
goal: By the end you can store and query a JSON document in a jsonb column without the text-comparison trap, index it for containment with GIN, ingest a message that may arrive twice at the same moment with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, and bring a summary table in line with its source in one MERGE.

warmup.q: Two Kafka consumers receive the same payment message at the same moment. Each runs `SELECT ... WHERE payment_uid = ?` and, if it finds nothing, `INSERT`s the payment. payment_uid has a UNIQUE constraint. What happens?
options: One consumer's SELECT waits for the other's INSERT, so the second consumer sees the row and skips it
Both checks find nothing; the second INSERT waits for the first transaction and then fails with a duplicate key error
Both inserts succeed, because each check passed
PostgreSQL merges the two inserts into one row
warmup.why: A SELECT never waits for an uncommitted INSERT: it reads committed data and finds nothing in both sessions. The unique index is what notices: the second INSERT finds the first one's uncommitted entry, waits for that transaction, and fails with 23505 once it commits. Without the unique constraint, the third option is what you would get: the same payment stored twice.

sections.h: A jsonb column stores a parsed document, so SQL can look inside it
sections.body:
Every payment carries what the risk engine said about it, and the shape of that keeps changing. A web payment gets a score and a list of rules that fired. Next month the fraud team adds a device fingerprint for mobile, then a 3-D Secure result. A column per field would mean a migration for every new rule, so `payments.metadata` holds the engine's JSON as it arrived:

```json
{"channel": "web", "risk": {"score": 91, "rules": ["velocity"]}}
```

The simplest version stores it as `text`, and then PostgreSQL knows nothing about it. A truncated document is stored without complaint, and every question becomes string matching: `metadata LIKE '%velocity%'` also matches a rule called `velocity_hourly`, or a note that mentions the word.

The `jsonb` type parses the text once, when you write it, and rejects anything that is not valid JSON. It stores the result as a binary tree of keys and values, so a query can walk straight to `risk`, then to `score`, without parsing the document again. The older `json` type keeps the original text, with its whitespace, key order and duplicate keys. `jsonb` normalizes it: keys come back in its own order, and of two equal keys only the last one survives. Use `jsonb` unless you must return the exact bytes you were sent.

Two operators walk into a document. `->` takes a key, or an array position, and returns jsonb: still a document. `->>` does the same and returns text. So `metadata -> 'risk' -> 'score'` is the jsonb number 91, and `metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score'` is the string `'91'`. In Kotlin terms, `->` is Jackson's `node.get("score")`, still a `JsonNode`, and `->>` is `node.get("score").asText()`.

The difference bites in comparisons. `metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score' > '50'` compares strings, character by character, and `'8' > '50'` because `'8'` sorts after `'5'`. On the 37 seeded payments it finds 14 high-risk payments, and six of them score 6 to 9. Cast before you compare: `(metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score')::int > 50` finds the right 8.

The operator to know best is containment, `@>`. `metadata @> '{"risk": {"rules": ["velocity"]}}'` asks whether the document contains that smaller document: a `risk` object whose `rules` array has the element `"velocity"`, whatever else is around it. It finds payments 3, 15 and 18, and never a rule that only starts with the same letters. Its cousin `?` asks whether a key, or a string element of an array, exists: `metadata -> 'risk' -> 'rules' ? 'velocity'`.

sections.h: A GIN index answers containment by looking up every key and value
sections.body:
The large data set has 478 near-duplicate payments, flagged in their metadata with `"injected_dup": true`. Finding them with `metadata @> '{"injected_dup": true}'` reads all 23,818 pages of payments, which takes between half a second and a few seconds depending on how busy Docker is.

A B-tree index (lesson 9 used one, and lesson 11 builds them up properly) cannot help. It sorts whole values, and "contains this key somewhere inside" is not a range of sorted documents. What helps is the kind of index at the back of a book: every word, with the pages it appears on. A **GIN index** (generalized inverted index) is exactly that. For every key and every value that occurs in any document, it keeps a sorted list of the rows that contain it. For `@>`, PostgreSQL looks up each key and value of the query document, intersects their row lists, and reads only those rows.

`CREATE INDEX payments_metadata_gin ON payments USING gin (metadata)` takes a few seconds and is under 9 MB, against 186 MB for the table. The same query becomes a Bitmap Index Scan on the GIN index and reads 17 pages: 3 of the index and the 14 table pages where the 478 rows live. It takes under a millisecond. The plan shows a `Recheck Cond` because the default GIN index stores keys and values without how they nest, so PostgreSQL checks each candidate row against the full condition.

Two limits. A GIN index on `metadata` serves only the jsonb operators `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&`, `@?` and `@@`. `metadata ->> 'injected_dup' = 'true'` means the same as the containment query and still reads every page, because `->>` produces text that the index does not hold. Write containment. And an index helps only when it lets PostgreSQL read less: the velocity rule fired on 5% of payments, 50,188 rows spread over 21,036 of the 23,818 pages, and counting them through the GIN index was slower than the sequential scan, since it visited almost every page anyway.

If you only ever query with `@>`, `USING gin (metadata jsonb_path_ops)` builds a smaller index, 4.5 MB here. It supports `@>`, `@?` and `@@`, and not the key-exists operators.

sections.h: Check, then insert, lets one message in twice
sections.body:
The card network delivers each payment message at least once. A Kafka consumer that crashes before it commits its offset gets the same message again after the rebalance, sometimes while the first consumer is still working on it. `payment_uid` is the network's idempotency key, so the ingest must store each uid once. The obvious code checks first:

```kotlin
if (payments.findByUid(msg.uid) == null) {     // both consumers: not found
    payments.insert(msg)                       // both consumers: insert
}
```

Two consumers can both run the check before either inserts. Both find nothing, and both insert. Without a unique constraint on payment_uid, that stores one payment twice, and settlement pays the merchant twice. The course schema has the constraint (`payment_uid uuid NOT NULL UNIQUE`), and it saves you. The second `INSERT` finds the first consumer's uncommitted entry in the unique index and waits for that transaction to end. If it commits, the second fails with `duplicate key value violates unique constraint`, SQLSTATE 23505. If it rolls back, the second goes through. Either way, one row.

Catching that error is clumsy. An error aborts the transaction it happens in, so a consumer that stores a batch of 500 messages in one transaction loses all 500 to one duplicate, unless it wraps each insert in a savepoint.

`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO NOTHING` moves the decision into the statement. The insert consults the unique index itself, in the same step as the write. When the key is already there, or is being inserted by a transaction still in progress (it waits for that one first), it skips the row instead of failing. Add `RETURNING payment_id` and you learn which happened: one row back means inserted, none means a repeat. For the DO UPDATE form, the PostgreSQL docs guarantee an insert or an update "even under high concurrency", and the stepper shows DO NOTHING holding up the same way.

That is the picture for this lesson: **the unique index is the referee**. A check in a separate statement answers a question that can be out of date before you act on it. Only a write that consults the index as it happens is safe against a twin arriving in the same millisecond. In Kotlin terms, check-then-insert is `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map[k] = v`, and `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` is `ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent(k, v)`.

frames.say: Had A crashed or rolled back instead, its entry would vanish and B's INSERT would insert the payment itself. Every interleaving ends with exactly one row, because the decision is taken by the unique index at the moment of the write, not by a check that ran earlier.

try.title: Race two inserts
steps: Open two terminals in the `labs` folder and run psql in both: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`. Call them A and B. Start the database first if it is not running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`).
Run part 1, switching terminals at each comment. B's INSERT hangs until A commits: what does it print then?
Run part 2 the same way. What does B's INSERT return after A's COMMIT?

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course

try.expect:
In part 1 both counts are 0, and B's INSERT prints nothing until A commits. Then:

```postgresql
-- B
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "payments_payment_uid_key"
DETAIL:  Key (payment_uid)=(019f1d1f-0500-7000-8000-0000000a0001) already exists.
23505
```

In part 2, A's INSERT returns one row, and B's waits again. When A commits, B's finishes without an error:

```postgresql
-- B
 payment_id
------------
(0 rows)

INSERT 0 0
```

The final SELECT shows a single pending payment. Its payment_id was 40 on a fresh database: part 1 used up 38 and 39, although only one of those inserts survived, and B's skipped insert in part 2 took 41. Each part deletes the payment again, so the seed stays as it was.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: INSERT, the ON CONFLICT clause

sections.h: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE turns the second message into an update
sections.body:
Not every repeat is a duplicate. Payment 20 is `pending`: the network authorized it and will send the capture later, a second message with the same uid and the status `succeeded`. This time the conflict should update the row:

```sql
INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)
VALUES ('019d0ab9-28c0-7014-8000-000000000014', 3, 1, 7425, 'succeeded', '2026-03-20 10:10+00')
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE
SET status = EXCLUDED.status
WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending'
RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status AS old_status, new.status AS new_status;
```

`EXCLUDED` is the row the INSERT proposed and could not insert. The `WHERE` decides whether the existing row changes at all. Without it, a late `pending`, an authorization message that arrives after its capture, would set a succeeded payment back to pending. With it, only a pending payment moves, and only to a final status. Any other repeat leaves the row alone and returns nothing.

`RETURNING old.status, new.status` is new in PostgreSQL 18: `old` is the row before the statement and `new` the row after. For an insert, `old` is all NULL; for an update, both are filled. One statement now tells the consumer what it did: inserted, updated, or nothing.

Three rules decide whether the statement works at all:

- The conflict target names a unique index or constraint. `ON CONFLICT (payment_uid)` works because payment_uid is UNIQUE; a clash on any other unique index, the primary key for example, still raises an error.
- One statement may not change the same row twice. A batch that carries one uid twice fails with `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time`, so deduplicate the batch first.
- Every attempted insert takes a value from the payment_id sequence, including the ones that end in a conflict. Ids get gaps, so never use them as a count.

`DO UPDATE` writes a new version of the row, as every UPDATE does (lesson 1), even when the new values equal the old ones. The `WHERE` saves those writes too.

try.title: Capture, repeat, late message, new payment
steps: Start the database if it is not running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, from the `labs` folder) and open psql: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`. Type `\pset null '∅'` if you have not.
Run the block one statement at a time and predict each result before you run it.
Statement 5 fails on purpose. The ROLLBACK at the end undoes everything.

code.title: psql, database course
code.src:
\pset null '∅'
BEGIN;
-- 1. the capture for payment 20, which is pending
INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)
VALUES ('019d0ab9-28c0-7014-8000-000000000014', 3, 1, 7425, 'succeeded', '2026-03-20 10:10+00')
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE
SET status = EXCLUDED.status
WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending'
RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status AS old_status, new.status AS new_status;

-- 2. the same capture again
INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)
VALUES ('019d0ab9-28c0-7014-8000-000000000014', 3, 1, 7425, 'succeeded', '2026-03-20 10:10+00')
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE
SET status = EXCLUDED.status
WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending'
RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status AS old_status, new.status AS new_status;

-- 3. a late 'pending' for the same payment, without the WHERE guard
INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)
VALUES ('019d0ab9-28c0-7014-8000-000000000014', 3, 1, 7425, 'pending', '2026-03-20 10:10+00')
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE
SET status = EXCLUDED.status
RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status AS old_status, new.status AS new_status;

-- 4. a payment nobody has seen
INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)
VALUES ('019f1d1f-0500-7000-8000-0000000a0001', 1, 1, 4200, 'pending', '2026-07-01 10:00+00')
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE
SET status = EXCLUDED.status
WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending'
RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status AS old_status, new.status AS new_status;

-- 5. one batch that carries payment 20 twice
INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)
VALUES ('019d0ab9-28c0-7014-8000-000000000014', 3, 1, 7425, 'succeeded', '2026-03-20 10:10+00'),
       ('019d0ab9-28c0-7014-8000-000000000014', 3, 1, 7425, 'failed',    '2026-03-20 10:10+00')
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE
SET status = EXCLUDED.status;
ROLLBACK;

try.expect:
```postgresql
 payment_id | old_status | new_status
------------+------------+------------
         20 | pending    | succeeded
(1 row)

 payment_id | old_status | new_status
------------+------------+------------
(0 rows)

 payment_id | old_status | new_status
------------+------------+------------
         20 | succeeded  | pending
(1 row)

 payment_id | old_status | new_status
------------+------------+------------
         45 | ∅          | pending
(1 row)

ERROR:  ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time
HINT:  Ensure that no rows proposed for insertion within the same command have duplicate constrained values.
```

Statement 2 changed nothing, so it returned nothing. Statement 3, without the guard, moved a succeeded payment back to pending: that is the bug the WHERE prevents. The new payment got id 45 on a fresh database after the previous Try it: statements 1 to 3 each used up a sequence value though none inserted a row. The ROLLBACK undoes all of it.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18 release notes: OLD and NEW in RETURNING

sections.h: MERGE brings a table in line with its source in one statement
sections.body:
Every night a job recomputes each merchant's monthly gross from the succeeded payments into `merchant_month_totals (merchant_id, month, gross_minor, payment_count)`. Since the last run, three things can have happened to a month. A merchant's first payment came in: a row to insert. A late payment arrived: a row to correct. A payment was reversed and the merchant has no sales left that month: a row to delete. `ON CONFLICT` can insert and update, but it cannot delete. `MERGE` does all three in one statement:

```sql
MERGE INTO merchant_month_totals AS t
USING (SELECT merchant_id, date '2026-02-01' AS month,
              sum(amount_minor) AS gross_minor, count(*) AS payment_count
       FROM payments
       WHERE status = 'succeeded' AND created_at >= '2026-02-01' AND created_at < '2026-03-01'
       GROUP BY merchant_id) AS s
ON t.merchant_id = s.merchant_id AND t.month = s.month
WHEN MATCHED AND (t.gross_minor, t.payment_count) IS DISTINCT FROM (s.gross_minor, s.payment_count) THEN
    UPDATE SET gross_minor = s.gross_minor, payment_count = s.payment_count
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT VALUES (s.merchant_id, s.month, s.gross_minor, s.payment_count)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.month = date '2026-02-01' THEN
    DELETE
RETURNING merge_action(), t.merchant_id, old.gross_minor, new.gross_minor;
```

MERGE joins the target to the source on the `ON` condition and puts every row into one of three classes. MATCHED rows are on both sides. NOT MATCHED rows are only in the source. NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE rows are only in the target; that clause came in PostgreSQL 17. For each row, the first WHEN clause whose class and extra condition fit decides what happens. A matched row whose numbers already agree fits no clause and is left alone.

Mind the condition on the DELETE. The source holds February only, so every January row is "not matched by source" too. Leave out `AND t.month = ...` and the MERGE deletes all of January, as the Try it shows. `RETURNING` on MERGE, with `merge_action()` to say which branch produced each row, came in PostgreSQL 17, and PostgreSQL 18 added `old` and `new`. If two source rows match the same target row, MERGE fails with `MERGE command cannot affect row a second time`.

MERGE has one weakness. It sorts rows into MATCHED and NOT MATCHED from its snapshot, and it has no arbiter index that makes a concurrent insert of the same key wait. When two sessions merge the same new (merchant, month) at once, the second fails with 23505, and the PostgreSQL docs point to `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` for concurrent upserts. Use MERGE for a batch sync that one job runs at a time, and ON CONFLICT for messages that can arrive twice at once.

try.title: Sync February's totals
steps: Start the database if it is not running (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`, from the `labs` folder) and open psql: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`.
Run the block. It creates a totals table inside a transaction, fills it with last night's numbers for January and February, and merges February's payments into it.
Before the second MERGE, predict which rows it will delete.

code.title: psql, database course
code.src:
\pset null '∅'
BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE merchant_month_totals (
    merchant_id    bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES merchants,
    month          date   NOT NULL,
    gross_minor    bigint NOT NULL,
    payment_count  int    NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, month)
);
INSERT INTO merchant_month_totals VALUES
    (1, '2026-01-01',   4250, 1), (4, '2026-01-01', 129900, 1),
    (1, '2026-02-01',   6120, 1),     -- payment 11 arrived after last night's run
    (2, '2026-02-01',   3400, 1),     -- payment 10 was later reported failed
    (4, '2026-02-01',  54999, 1),
    (7, '2026-02-01',   1450, 1);     -- merchant 3 has no February row yet

MERGE INTO merchant_month_totals AS t
USING (SELECT merchant_id, date '2026-02-01' AS month,
              sum(amount_minor) AS gross_minor, count(*) AS payment_count
       FROM payments
       WHERE status = 'succeeded'
         AND created_at >= '2026-02-01' AND created_at < '2026-03-01'
       GROUP BY merchant_id) AS s
ON t.merchant_id = s.merchant_id AND t.month = s.month
WHEN MATCHED AND (t.gross_minor, t.payment_count) IS DISTINCT FROM (s.gross_minor, s.payment_count) THEN
    UPDATE SET gross_minor = s.gross_minor, payment_count = s.payment_count
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (merchant_id, month, gross_minor, payment_count)
    VALUES (s.merchant_id, s.month, s.gross_minor, s.payment_count)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.month = date '2026-02-01' THEN
    DELETE
RETURNING merge_action() AS action, t.merchant_id, t.month,
          old.gross_minor AS old_gross, new.gross_minor AS new_gross;

SELECT * FROM merchant_month_totals ORDER BY month, merchant_id;

-- the same MERGE without "AND t.month = ..." on the DELETE branch
MERGE INTO merchant_month_totals AS t
USING (SELECT merchant_id, date '2026-02-01' AS month,
              sum(amount_minor) AS gross_minor, count(*) AS payment_count
       FROM payments
       WHERE status = 'succeeded'
         AND created_at >= '2026-02-01' AND created_at < '2026-03-01'
       GROUP BY merchant_id) AS s
ON t.merchant_id = s.merchant_id AND t.month = s.month
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN
    DELETE
RETURNING merge_action() AS action, t.merchant_id, t.month;
ROLLBACK;

try.expect:
```postgresql
 action | merchant_id |   month    | old_gross | new_gross
--------+-------------+------------+-----------+-----------
 UPDATE |           1 | 2026-02-01 |      6120 |      8620
 DELETE |           2 | 2026-02-01 |      3400 |         ∅
 INSERT |           3 | 2026-02-01 |         ∅ |       275
(3 rows)

MERGE 3
```

Merchants 4 and 7 were already right and are not in the output: the `IS DISTINCT FROM` test left them alone. The SELECT shows the two January rows untouched and four February rows. The second MERGE, without the month test, returns `DELETE | 1 | 2026-01-01` and `DELETE | 4 | 2026-01-01`: it deleted January because January is not in February's source. The ROLLBACK removes the table again.

analogy: The unique index is the doorman with the guest list. Check-then-insert is two friends each phoning the venue to ask whether a name is on the list, both hearing no, and both turning up to write it in. ON CONFLICT is walking up to the doorman, who checks and writes in one movement; if someone ahead of you is writing the same name, you wait, and then he tells you the name is already in. MERGE is the manager going through the whole list against the booking system at the end of the night: add the missing names, correct the misspelled ones, cross out the cancellations. jsonb is the guest's form filled in on the venue's own template, so anyone can find the dietary field without reading the whole letter. The analogy breaks on timing: a real doorman serves one person at a time, while PostgreSQL lets thousands of inserts with different keys go through the same index at once and only makes the ones with the same key wait.
in_your_world: Every Kafka consumer that writes to a database is at-least-once, so its write must be idempotent: an upsert keyed on the message's idempotency key, inside the same transaction as the business change, and the offset committed after the database commit. A Temporal activity that stores a payment needs the same thing, because Temporal retries an activity after a timeout even when the first attempt reached the database. On Oracle there is no ON CONFLICT, so the upsert is a MERGE, and two sessions merging the same new key can still collide with ORA-00001; catch it and retry, or insert first and treat the duplicate key error as "already done". Beware of JPA's EntityManager.merge(): it loads the entity and then inserts or updates, which is check-then-insert with the same race. For the risk engine's payloads, a jsonb column with a GIN index lets the fraud team query new fields the day they appear, and it is no excuse to keep the amount, the status or the merchant inside JSON: those stay real columns with real constraints.
mistake: Making an ingest idempotent with a lookup before the insert: findByUid, then insert if absent, or a NOT EXISTS subquery in the INSERT. It works in every test, because tests deliver one message at a time, and it fails in production when a rebalance or a retry delivers the same message to two workers at once: both checks pass, and either the unique constraint throws a duplicate key error that aborts the whole batch, or, without the constraint, the payment is stored twice. The fix is to let the write itself consult the unique index: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO NOTHING, or DO UPDATE with a WHERE that only moves a row forward, and RETURNING to learn what happened.

compare.title: An idempotent upsert of one payment message: Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle: MERGE is the upsert
a.src:
MERGE INTO payments p
USING (SELECT :uid AS payment_uid, :card AS card_id,
              :merchant AS merchant_id, :amount AS amount_minor,
              :status AS status, :created AS created_at
       FROM dual) m
ON (p.payment_uid = m.payment_uid)
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET p.status = m.status
    WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND m.status <> 'pending'
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id,
            amount_minor, status, created_at)
    VALUES (m.payment_uid, m.card_id, m.merchant_id,
            m.amount_minor, m.status, m.created_at);
-- two sessions inserting the same new uid at once:
-- the second can fail with ORA-00001; catch and retry

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT
b.src:
INSERT INTO payments AS p
       (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id,
        amount_minor, status, created_at)
VALUES (:uid, :card, :merchant,
        :amount, :status, :created)
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE
SET status = EXCLUDED.status
WHERE p.status = 'pending'
  AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending'
RETURNING p.payment_id,
          old.status, new.status;
-- a concurrent insert of the same uid makes this
-- one wait, then take the DO UPDATE branch:
-- no error to catch

compare.note: Oracle has no ON CONFLICT clause, so Oracle code spells the upsert as a MERGE against a one-row source, often from DUAL. PostgreSQL has MERGE too, since version 15, and the same race: MERGE decides MATCHED or NOT MATCHED before it writes, so two concurrent MERGEs of the same new key can both choose INSERT, and the unique index rejects the second. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT is different because the unique index arbitrates inside the write: the second session waits for the first and then takes the DO UPDATE or DO NOTHING branch. The WHERE clause on the update branch exists in both, and does the same job: a late message never moves a payment backward. PostgreSQL 18 adds RETURNING old and new on both statements, which Oracle 23ai also added for UPDATE and MERGE.

worked.title: An idempotent Kafka batch: one statement, one round trip

steps.say: The consumer polls 500 messages. They may repeat each other (the producer retried), repeat payments already stored (a rebalance redelivered them), or bring the capture of a pending payment. First collapse repeats inside the batch, keeping a final status over `pending`, because one statement may not touch the same row twice:
steps.code:
// 1. one message per uid; a final status beats 'pending'
val batch = records.map { it.value() }                        // List<PaymentMessage>
    .sortedByDescending { it.status != "pending" }             // final statuses first
    .distinctBy { it.uid }                                     // keeps the first of each uid

steps.say: Send the whole batch as arrays and unnest them into rows on the server: one statement and one network round trip for 500 messages, instead of 500. The ON CONFLICT clause is the one from this lesson.
steps.code:
-- 2. the statement: unnest turns six arrays into rows
INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)
SELECT * FROM unnest(?::uuid[], ?::bigint[], ?::bigint[], ?::bigint[], ?::text[], ?::timestamptz[])
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE
SET status = EXCLUDED.status
WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending'
RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status, new.status

steps.say: Bind each column as a JDBC array. The rows that come back are exactly the changes: an insert has a NULL old status, a capture has `pending`, and repeats return nothing.

Commit the database first and the Kafka offset second. If the consumer dies between the two, Kafka redelivers the batch, and the upsert turns every message in it into a no-op. At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent write is how you get each payment stored exactly once.

lab.title: The fraud queue, an idempotent ingest and the monthly MERGE
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the `labs` folder. Seven of the eight fail. The one that passes inserts a new message twice, one delivery after the other, which the placeholder handles; its trouble starts when two deliveries overlap.

`risky_payments.sql` compares the score as text and searches the document as a string. Return the payments with a score of 50 or more, or with the velocity rule, comparing numbers and using containment.

`ingest_payment.sql` reads messages from a temporary table `inbound` and checks before it inserts. Make it one INSERT ... ON CONFLICT statement that inserts new payments, moves a pending payment to its final status, ignores everything else, and returns one row per change. One test runs it in two sessions at the same moment.
`settle_month.sql` is a MERGE that rewrites every March row, even correct ones, and deletes every month that March's source lacks. Make it change only the March rows that are wrong, missing or gone.

Run the tests until all eight pass. The second test of each exercise adds rows first: a high score of 100 and a rule named velocity_hourly, a batch mixing new, repeated, late and final messages, and new March payments next to a February one.
hints: `WHERE (metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score')::int >= 50 OR metadata @> '{"risk": {"rules": ["velocity"]}}'`. A document without a score gives NULL for the cast, which is neither >= 50 nor an error.

`INSERT INTO payments AS p (...) SELECT ... FROM inbound ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status WHERE p.status = 'pending' AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending' RETURNING p.payment_id, old.status AS old_status, new.status AS new_status`.
Add `AND (t.gross_minor, t.payment_count) IS DISTINCT FROM (s.gross_minor, s.payment_count)` to WHEN MATCHED, and `AND t.month = date '2026-03-01'` to WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE.

drill.title: The ingest statement, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the statement that stores one payment message (uid, card, merchant, amount, status, created_at) so that a repeat changes nothing, a capture moves a pending payment to its final status, a late 'pending' never moves a payment backward, and the statement reports whether it inserted, updated or did nothing. Then write the query for the payments whose risk rules include "geo_mismatch", in a form a GIN index on metadata can serve.

answer.src:
INSERT INTO payments AS p (payment_uid, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6)
ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO UPDATE          -- the unique index decides, even mid-race
SET status = EXCLUDED.status                 -- EXCLUDED: the row the INSERT proposed
WHERE p.status = 'pending'                   -- only pending payments move,
  AND EXCLUDED.status <> 'pending'           -- and only forward
RETURNING p.payment_id,
          old.status AS old_status,          -- NULL: inserted
          new.status AS new_status;          -- no row at all: a repeat

SELECT payment_id
FROM payments
WHERE metadata @> '{"risk": {"rules": ["geo_mismatch"]}}';   -- containment: GIN can answer it
-- payments 8 and 31 on the seed

recap: jsonb parses JSON once on write, rejects invalid documents and lets SQL walk inside: -> returns jsonb, ->> returns text. Compare ->> results as text only when you mean text; cast numbers first.
@> asks whether a document contains a smaller one. A GIN index lists every key and value with the rows that hold it, so containment reads only matching rows; ->> conditions cannot use it.
Check-then-insert is a race: two sessions both find nothing. The unique index is the referee, and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT asks it in the same step as the write.
ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET ... = EXCLUDED.col WHERE ... updates only when the row should move; PostgreSQL 18's RETURNING old and new says what happened. One statement cannot touch the same row twice.

MERGE inserts, updates and deletes against a source in one statement (NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE since 17, RETURNING since 17, old and new since 18). Guard its DELETE, and use ON CONFLICT when two sessions may write the same new key at once.

quiz.q: Which scores does `WHERE metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score' >= '70'` let through?
options: Only scores of 70 and above
70 to 99, and also 8 and 9, but not 100
Every score, because text sorts after numbers
None: comparing text with a number raises an error
quiz.why: ->> returns text, and '70' is a text literal, so PostgreSQL compares strings character by character: '8' and '9' sort after '7', and '100' sorts before it because '1' < '7'. Cast first, `(metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score')::int >= 70`, or compare jsonb with jsonb, `metadata -> 'risk' -> 'score' >= '70'`, which compares numbers.

quiz.q: payments has `CREATE INDEX ... USING gin (metadata)`. Which condition can the index serve?
options: `metadata ->> 'channel' = 'pos'`
`(metadata -> 'risk' ->> 'score')::int > 90`
`metadata::text LIKE '%pos%'`
`metadata @> '{"channel": "pos"}'`
quiz.why: A GIN index on a jsonb column serves the jsonb operators such as @>, ? and @?. The other three apply a function or a cast to the column first, so they produce values the index does not contain, and the plan is a sequential scan. The first one asks the same question as the containment query; only the containment form can use the index.

quiz.q: Session A runs `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO NOTHING RETURNING payment_id` for a new uid and has not committed. Session B runs the same statement for the same uid. What does B see?
options: B waits; when A commits, B's statement returns no rows and no error
B returns no rows at once, because A's row is already in the index
B inserts a second row, because A has not committed
B fails with a duplicate key error when A commits
quiz.why: B finds A's uncommitted entry in the unique index and cannot know yet whether A will commit, so it waits. When A commits, B takes the DO NOTHING branch: no rows, no error. Had A rolled back, B would have inserted. The duplicate key error is what a plain INSERT, without ON CONFLICT, gets in the same situation.

quiz.q: A nightly MERGE syncs March's totals with `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE` and no further condition. The target holds rows for January, February and March. What does it delete?
options: Only March rows whose merchant had no March payments
Nothing, because NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE needs a condition to run
Every January and February row, plus the March rows with no March payments
Only rows of merchants with no payments at all
quiz.why: The source holds only March, so every January and February row has no source match and falls in NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE. Without a condition such as `AND t.month = date '2026-03-01'`, the DELETE applies to all of them. The clause runs without a condition; that is exactly the danger.

quiz.q: A Kafka batch carries some payment_uids more than once, because the producer retried, and the upsert fails with "cannot affect row a second time". Which source query keeps one row per uid, the most recently received?
options: `SELECT DISTINCT payment_uid, status, received_at FROM batch`
`SELECT DISTINCT ON (payment_uid) * FROM batch ORDER BY payment_uid, received_at DESC`
`SELECT payment_uid, max(status), max(received_at) FROM batch GROUP BY payment_uid`
`SELECT * FROM batch ORDER BY received_at DESC LIMIT 1`
quiz.why: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each uid in the ORDER BY, here the latest, as lesson 9 did for the latest login. DISTINCT over all columns keeps all three rows, because their statuses differ. max() of each column mixes values from different rows, the trap of lesson 9's latest_login exercise. LIMIT 1 keeps one row for the whole batch.

flashcards.back: jsonb: parsed once on write, validated, stored as a tree, indexable. json keeps the exact text, including duplicate keys.
-> returns jsonb (still a document), ->> returns text. Cast ->> results before comparing numbers.
Whether doc contains that smaller document: a risk object whose rules array includes "velocity".

flashcards.front: Which conditions can a GIN index on a jsonb column serve?
flashcards.back: The jsonb operators: @>, ?, ?|, ?& and the jsonpath ones @? and @@. Not ->> comparisons.

flashcards.front: Why is check-then-insert unsafe, and what replaces it?
flashcards.back: Two sessions can both find nothing before either inserts. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT lets the unique index decide inside the write.

flashcards.front: In ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, what is EXCLUDED?
flashcards.back: The row the INSERT proposed and could not insert, so SET status = EXCLUDED.status takes the new message's value.

flashcards.front: Why prefer ON CONFLICT over MERGE for concurrent upserts in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: MERGE has no arbiter index: two sessions merging the same new key can both choose INSERT, and one fails with 23505.

terms.plain: PostgreSQL's binary JSON type: parsed and validated on write, stored as a tree of keys and values.
The test of whether one JSON document contains another, nesting included.
Generalized inverted index: for every key and value, the sorted list of rows that contain it.
A unique id that the sender attaches to a message so the receiver can tell a repeat from a new request.
Insert a row, or update it if a row with the same key already exists, as one atomic operation.
In ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, the row that was proposed for insertion.
A statement that joins a target to a source and inserts, updates or deletes target rows by class: matched, not matched, not matched by source.
A function in MERGE ... RETURNING that says which action produced the row: INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate's Kafka consumer stores payments with `if (repo.findByUid(uid) == null) repo.insert(msg)` inside a transaction per batch. It passes every test, but once a week a batch fails with a duplicate key error and is retried. Explain what is happening and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: The weekly failure is two deliveries of the same message overlapping, usually after a rebalance or a producer retry. Each transaction runs its findByUid before the other has committed, so both see nothing and both insert. The unique constraint on payment_uid catches it: the second insert waits for the first transaction and then fails with 23505. Because the error aborts the whole transaction, the consumer loses the entire batch and retries it, and if the constraint were missing, the payment would simply be stored twice. Tests never show this because they deliver one message at a time. I would remove the check and let the insert consult the unique index itself: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (payment_uid) DO NOTHING, or DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status WHERE the stored payment is still pending and the message carries a final status, with RETURNING to know whether it inserted, updated or did nothing. The second session then waits and takes the conflict branch instead of failing. I would also deduplicate the batch by uid before sending it, since one statement may not touch the same row twice, and commit the Kafka offset only after the database commit, so a crash in between means a harmless redelivery.

deeper.body:
`DO NOTHING` does not return the existing row, so a caller that needs the id of a repeat has to run a second query: `SELECT payment_id FROM payments WHERE payment_uid = $1`. A common workaround is `DO UPDATE SET status = p.status`, an update that changes nothing so that RETURNING has a row, but it writes a new row version on every repeat. PostgreSQL 19, at release candidate as this lesson is written, adds `ON CONFLICT DO SELECT`, which returns the conflicting row, optionally locking it.

`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` locks the conflicting row while it updates it, so concurrent upserts of one key queue up one behind the other. That is what you want for a capture racing its own repeat. It also means a very hot key, such as a single counter row upserted by every request, becomes a queue: see lesson 13 for row locks and their waits.

Before PostgreSQL 18 there was no `old` in RETURNING, and people told inserts from updates with `RETURNING (xmax = 0) AS inserted`: a freshly inserted row version has no deleting transaction recorded. It works, but it reads a system column whose meaning is an implementation detail. Use `old` on 18.

PostgreSQL 17 brought the SQL/JSON standard functions. `JSON_TABLE` turns a document into rows and typed columns inside FROM, the standard spelling of what lesson 9 did with `jsonb_array_elements_text`:

```sql
SELECT p.payment_id, r.rule
FROM payments p,
     JSON_TABLE(p.metadata, '$.risk.rules[*]' COLUMNS (rule text PATH '$')) AS r
ORDER BY p.payment_id;
-- 3 velocity, 8 geo_mismatch, 15 velocity, 18 velocity, 31 geo_mismatch
```

jsonpath, the small query language inside that `'$.risk.rules[*]'`, also works with the `@?` operator: `metadata @? '$.risk.score ? (@ > 50)'` finds the same 8 payments as the cast, and a GIN index can serve it.

A unique index on an expression works as a conflict target too. For case-insensitive emails, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON customers (lower(email))` and then `ON CONFLICT ((lower(email))) DO NOTHING`.
